title: 1 Chronicles 8:1–28
context: Chapter 8 returns to Benjamin with a fuller list than 7:6–12, kept here as one large unit. The sons of Benjamin are named differently than in 7:6 and Genesis 46:21, and the text does not explain the differences. The list includes movements and conflicts: a deportation from Geba to Manahath (8:6–7), children born in the field of Moab (8:8), the building of Ono and Lod (8:12), and men of Aijalon who put the people of Gath to flight (8:13). Verses 6–8 are terse and difficult to follow, and this page does not reconstruct them. Readers have asked whether the Ehud of 8:6 is the judge Ehud, whom Judges 3:15 calls “the son of Gera, the Benjamite”; Gera does appear in 8:3, 5, but the text does not make the identification. The unit closes with heads of households who lived in Jerusalem (8:28). Both traditions read it as shared ground: Benjamin, the tribe of Saul, remained part of God’s people and had a place in Jerusalem.

verses.text: Benjamin became the father of Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, Aharah the third,
verses.arminianNotes: Benjamin’s sons begin with Bela his firstborn, Ashbel, and Aharah. Arminian readers note that this fuller Benjamin list differs from 7:6 and Genesis 46:21, and they accept that genealogies could serve different purposes. The Chronicler gives Benjamin special attention.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the different lists without forcing a harmony. Benjamin’s prominence suits its role as Saul’s tribe and as a tribe that stayed with Judah. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing a fuller record of a tribe important to the returned community.

verses.text: Nohah the fourth, and Rapha the fifth.
verses.arminianNotes: Nohah and Rapha complete the five sons. Arminian readers note the orderly numbering, first through fifth, which gives the list a clear structure. Each son founded a family with its own place among the people, and the record honors that heritage before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the ordered list and its difference from other Benjamin genealogies, which the text does not explain. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical structure and decline to make the differing counts a point of theological dispute.

verses.text: Bela had sons: Addar, Gera, Abihud,
verses.arminianNotes: Bela’s sons begin with Addar, Gera, and Abihud. Arminian readers note that Gera is a name tied to Benjamin elsewhere, including the father of the judge Ehud (Judges 3:15), though they do not assume the same man is meant here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the familiar name and avoid hasty identification. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Bela’s family record and see in the recurring names the continuity of Benjamite families across generations.

verses.text: Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah,
verses.arminianNotes: Abishua, Naaman, and Ahoah continue Bela’s sons. Arminian readers note that Naaman also appears in Benjamin’s line in Genesis 46:21 and Numbers 26:40. The overlap reflects shared tradition behind the various lists, even where they differ in arrangement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the overlap and treat the differences calmly. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail that links this list with earlier records, and neither draws doctrinal conclusions from the arrangement of names.

verses.text: Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram.
verses.arminianNotes: Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram complete Bela’s sons. Arminian readers note that the name Gera appears twice in this list, which the text does not explain. They accept that ancient genealogies sometimes repeat names without telling us why.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the repetition and do not speculate beyond the text. Shephuphan resembles a name in Numbers 26:39. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of a careful but not fully explained record and affirm its value without forcing it.

verses.text: These are the sons of Ehud. These are the heads of fathers’ households of the inhabitants of Geba, who were carried captive to Manahath:
verses.arminianNotes: “These are the sons of Ehud,” heads of households in Geba who were carried captive to Manahath. Arminian readers note that the verse is difficult to connect with what precedes. Some ask whether this is the judge Ehud, but the text does not say, and they leave it open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the difficulty and avoid confident reconstruction. The mention of captivity shows that displacement was part of Benjamin’s history long before Babylon. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse cautiously and see God’s people preserved through upheaval.

verses.text: Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera, who carried them captive; and he became the father of Uzza and Ahihud.
verses.arminianNotes: Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera are named, with Gera described as the one who carried them captive. Arminian readers acknowledge that the verse is terse and hard to follow. They do not try to reconstruct the events, and they read it as a record of family movement and conflict.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the verse as obscure and decline to fill in details the text does not give. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with restraint and see in it a reminder that the history of God’s people includes displacement and difficult events.

verses.text: Shaharaim became the father of children in the field of Moab, after he had sent them away. Hushim and Baara were his wives.
verses.arminianNotes: Shaharaim has children in the field of Moab after sending away his wives Hushim and Baara. Arminian readers note the plain record of a family broken and rebuilt in a foreign land. The text records these events without commenting on them morally.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the honest account of a complicated household and the link with Moab. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical description and decline to moralize beyond the text, while noting that Israel’s families lived through real disruption.

verses.text: By Hodesh his wife, he became the father of Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam,
verses.arminianNotes: By his wife Hodesh, Shaharaim fathers Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, and Malcam. Arminian readers note that Mesha shares his name with a later king of Moab (2 Kings 3:4), which fits a family born in Moab, though the text does not comment on the names.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the setting in Moab and avoid drawing firm conclusions from the names. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail from a family living among neighboring peoples, still counted within the tribe of Benjamin.

verses.text: Jeuz, Shachia, and Mirmah. These were his sons, heads of fathers’ households.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeuz, Shachia, and Mirmah complete the sons of Hodesh, all heads of households. Arminian readers note that the family, though born in Moab, produced leaders within Benjamin. Living abroad did not remove them from the covenant people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God preserving the family’s place in Israel despite its time in Moab. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as evidence that God’s people remained his people even when scattered, a theme that would encourage the community after exile.

verses.text: By Hushim, he became the father of Abitub and Elpaal.
verses.arminianNotes: By Hushim, Shaharaim fathers Abitub and Elpaal. Arminian readers note that Elpaal will head a significant line in the following verses. The text shows the family’s continuation through more than one mother, recorded plainly as part of its history.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the transition to Elpaal’s line and the honest record of the household. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical connection and see in it the continuity of Benjamin’s families through complex circumstances.

verses.text: The sons of Elpaal: Eber, Misham, and Shemed, who built Ono and Lod, with its towns;
verses.arminianNotes: Elpaal’s sons include those who built Ono and Lod with its towns. Arminian readers note the recognition of building work, which shows families taking initiative to establish settlements. Their labor is remembered as part of Benjamin’s heritage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the building of towns and see God establishing his people in the land through their work. Ono and Lod are also mentioned among the returned exiles (Ezra 2:33). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as honoring the work of building community.

verses.text: and Beriah and Shema, who were heads of fathers’ households of the inhabitants of Aijalon, who put to flight the inhabitants of Gath;
verses.arminianNotes: Beriah and Shema, heads of households in Aijalon, put the inhabitants of Gath to flight. Arminian readers note the courage of these leaders in defending their people. The verse records a victory without detail, honoring their role in protecting the tribe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a record of deliverance from a hostile neighbor. The mention of Gath recalls the conflict in 7:21, though the text does not connect the two. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical record and see God’s protection working through faithful leaders.

verses.text: and Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth,
verses.arminianNotes: Ahio, Shashak, and Jeremoth begin a long list of names. Arminian readers note that these lists can be hard to follow, but each name marks a real person within Benjamin. The Chronicler preserves them to show the breadth of the tribe’s families in Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the list as testimony to the tribe’s size and continuity. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail and affirm that God’s concern reaches each household, even when the text records nothing beyond a name.

verses.text: Zebadiah, Arad, Eder,
verses.arminianNotes: Zebadiah, Arad, and Eder continue the list. Arminian readers note that some of these names also belong to places, a common feature of ancient genealogies. They read the verse simply as part of the family record of Benjamin, preserved with care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the verse as part of a careful record and do not press connections between names and places. Shared ground: both traditions read it as genealogical detail without theological controversy, and see value in the preservation of these families.

verses.text: Michael, Ishpah, Joha, the sons of Beriah,
verses.arminianNotes: Michael, Ishpah, and Joha are named as sons of Beriah. Arminian readers note that the list now groups names by father, making its structure clearer. Beriah’s family, already noted for its victory over Gath (8:13), continues to be remembered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the grouping and the continuity of Beriah’s line. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical structure and see in Beriah’s descendants the preservation of a family that served its people faithfully.

verses.text: Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, Heber,
verses.arminianNotes: Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, and Heber begin another group. Arminian readers note that common names like Meshullam recur often in Chronicles, so they avoid confusing this man with others of the same name. The record is about families, not famous individuals.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the frequency of such names and the care needed in reading them. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Benjamin’s record and affirm that ordinary, little-known people have a place in God’s story.

verses.text: Ishmerai, Izliah, Jobab, the sons of Elpaal,
verses.arminianNotes: Ishmerai, Izliah, and Jobab are named as sons of Elpaal. Arminian readers note that this completes the group linked to Elpaal (8:11–12), whose family included builders of towns. The record honors an extended household within the tribe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the completion of Elpaal’s line and its place among the heads of households. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical summary and see in it a testimony to the strength of Benjamin’s families.

verses.text: Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi,
verses.arminianNotes: Jakim, Zichri, and Zabdi begin another group of names. Arminian readers note the continuing list, which shows how many families made up Benjamin. They read it plainly, without seeking hidden meanings in the names themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as straightforward genealogy. Shared ground: both traditions see it as part of a careful record of Benjamin’s households and agree that it raises no doctrinal difference, while affirming God’s care for every family named.

verses.text: Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel,
verses.arminianNotes: Elienai, Zillethai, and Eliel continue the group. Arminian readers note that several names in this list appear to include a form of the Hebrew word for God, reflecting the faith expressed in Israelite naming. Parents named their children in ways that pointed to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the theological names and see in them a testimony to the faith of Israel’s families. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail and appreciate names that confess God, without building more on them than they can bear.

verses.text: Adaiah, Beraiah, Shimrath, the sons of Shimei,
verses.arminianNotes: Adaiah, Beraiah, and Shimrath are named as sons of Shimei. Arminian readers note the grouping by father once more. Shimei is a common name, and they do not assume a connection with other men of that name elsewhere in Scripture without clear evidence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the common name and avoid confusing this Shimei with others. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Benjamin’s family record, with no theological question raised, and affirm the value of each family preserved.

verses.text: Ishpan, Eber, Eliel,
verses.arminianNotes: Ishpan, Eber, and Eliel begin another group. Arminian readers note that the same names can recur within a single list, as Eliel does here and in 8:20, which reflects common naming patterns. The record stays faithful to the families it describes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the repetition of names and read it as normal in ancient genealogies. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse calmly as genealogical detail and decline to draw doctrinal conclusions from repeated names.

verses.text: Abdon, Zichri, Hanan,
verses.arminianNotes: Abdon, Zichri, and Hanan continue the list. Arminian readers note the steady record of names, which together testify to a large and established tribe in Jerusalem. Each name stands for a family with its own story, mostly unknown to us.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the list as evidence of God’s preservation of Benjamin. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the genealogy and affirm that God knows the stories behind the names, even when Scripture preserves only the names themselves.

verses.text: Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah,
verses.arminianNotes: Hananiah, Elam, and Anthothijah are named. Arminian readers note that Anthothijah may be connected with the town of Anathoth, though the text does not explain it. They read the name as part of the family record of Benjamin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the possible link cautiously. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail and see in the names the deep roots of Benjamin’s families in their land, without pressing connections the text does not state.

verses.text: Iphdeiah, Penuel, the sons of Shashak,
verses.arminianNotes: Iphdeiah and Penuel are named as sons of Shashak. Arminian readers note that the grouping completes the line of Shashak introduced in 8:14. The record continues to show the careful organization of the tribe’s households by father.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the completion of Shashak’s line. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical structure and agree that it raises no doctrinal question, while affirming the value of preserving these households within the people of God.

verses.text: Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah,
verses.arminianNotes: Shamsherai, Shehariah, and Athaliah begin the final group. Arminian readers note that Athaliah here is a man of Benjamin, not the queen of 2 Kings 11. Names could be shared by very different people, and the context makes clear who is meant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that this Athaliah is unrelated to the queen of Judah. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail and caution against confusing people who share a name, reading each in its own context.

verses.text: Jaareshiah, Elijah, Zichri, and the sons of Jeroham.
verses.arminianNotes: Jaareshiah, Elijah, and Zichri are named as sons of Jeroham. Arminian readers note that this Elijah is a Benjamite unrelated to the prophet. The list closes its groupings by father, completing the record of these households.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the common name and the completion of the groups. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail and see in the end of the list the careful preservation of Benjamin’s families in Jerusalem.

verses.text: These were heads of fathers’ households throughout their generations, chief men. These lived in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: These heads of households lived in Jerusalem. Arminian readers note that the long list ends by locating these families in the city where God’s house stood. Benjamin’s place in Jerusalem reflects its continuing role among God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same emphasis and note that Joshua 18:28 lists Jerusalem among Benjamin’s cities. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as connecting the genealogy with the holy city and see in it the importance of Jerusalem for the restored community.
